item.title: How Parents Can Both Contribute to and Prevent Sibling Abuse
item.description:
Domestic Violence

How Parents Can Both Contribute to and Prevent Sibling Abuse

Parents have a more powerful role in sibling abuse than they might think.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • An emotionally abusive family environment is the primary cause of sibling abuse.
  • Parents' behavior plays a key role in preventing sibling abuse.
  • Parents tend to downplay and minimize the damage caused by sibling abuse.

Until recently, sibling abuse has been overlooked as a major problem, especially compared to other forms of childhood abuse. The good news is that there has been a growing interest in this extremely damaging form of abuse. Extensive research shows that sibling abuse (emotional, physical, and sexual) can lead to internalized shame, substance abuse, self-harm, nightmares, phobias, delinquency, and running away. In addition, many victims suffer from long-term effects including chronic low self-esteem, distrusting others, eating disorders, an increased rate of depression and anxiety, substance abuse, difficulties with boundaries, and, most importantly, difficulties forming healthy relationships. Many experts now consider sibling abuse to be the least reported and most damaging type of childhood abuse. It has been reported that approximately one-third of children in the United States have been physically harmed, threatened, or humiliated by a sibling.

In this post, I will show how parents have much more power to stop sibling abuse from occurring than they are aware of. In fact, it is up to parents to prevent this damaging form of abuse in their own family.

Risk Factors for Sibling Abuse

The primary risk factor for sibling abuse is being raised in an emotionally abusive family. Specifically, exposure to parental conflict, family violence, and harsh parenting are linked to sibling abuse. Families living in chaos or continual crisis are at risk of sibling abuse, partly due to the fact that chaotic families create parental stress and overburdened parents, and these experiences of family stress are associated with higher rates of sibling aggression. A culture of violence in which children describe their family environment as a “battleground” is yet another factor. Living in such an environment, children learn to survive through intimidation and cruelty.

As I discovered while doing research for my latest book, Adult Children of Emotionally Abusive Families, children who witness one or both parents emotionally abusing each other are far more likely to pass the abuse on to a sibling. This is particularly true when the father has issues with control and anger. In essence, the abusive parent is acting as a role model for their children, sending this message: When you are angry or frustrated, it is OK to take that anger or frustration out on someone else, especially someone who is weaker or has less power. The same thing holds true when one or both parents emotionally, physically, or sexually abuse one or more children in the family. The abused child may then “pass on” the abuse toward a younger or weaker sibling.

There are many other precipitating factors when it comes to sibling abuse. These factors are all related to the environment in the home and the role that parents play in the child’s life. These factors include:

  • When parents confuse sibling abuse with sibling rivalry: Parents tend to ignore the problem and don’t help siblings resolve their conflicts by teaching them healthy conflict-resolution skills. This includes a parent’s inability to respond properly and parents normalizing abuse by ignoring or minimizing it. Silence and inaction can be taken as permission.
  • Studies show that there is a strong link between lack of supervision and the frequency and severity of sibling abuse. When children are left on their own, sibling abuse tends to occur more often, especially when an older child is left in charge of a younger one.
  • Parents not being available to meet their children’s emotional needs: For example, an emotionally neglected child may reach out to a sibling for the affection they long for, and this can lead to sibling sexual abuse.
  • When parents create a competitive environment in the home: In emotionally abusive families, parents tend to pit one child against the other, regularly compare siblings, favor one child over the others, and make one child the family scapegoat. This encourages sibling rivalry and eventually sibling abuse.
  • When siblings have to compete for available material and emotional resources (e.g., their parents’ attention), it can heighten the stress among siblings.
  • The inability of parents to set healthy boundaries among family members may also be a risk factor for sibling abuse.
  • Parents taking sides, blaming the victim, or shifting responsibility to the victim to resolve the issue (e.g., “Just stay out of his way.”)
  • A hierarchical family structure where one spouse controls the other, and older siblings (especially males) mimic that authoritarian behavior and attitude toward younger siblings, can cause sibling abuse. This includes cultural norms that condone abuse of power.
  • When a younger or weaker sibling is dependent on an older sibling for attention, support, or companionship, it gives the older sibling too much power.
  • When a child already has a history of being abused, either by other family members or someone outside the home, it makes them more vulnerable to sibling abuse.
  • And finally, when there are developmental, physical, or intellectual differences between siblings, the weaker sibling is more vulnerable to sibling abuse.
article continues after advertisement

The Role of Certain Parental Traits

In addition to the above circumstances, often the parents themselves—their personality traits (e.g., an aggressive temperament), their ways of coping, their belief systems—all contribute to the likelihood that sibling abuse will occur in the family. These include:

  • Overcontrolling parents
  • Parents who are alcohol- or drug-dependent: This is true for the following reasons: (1) Those under the influence of alcohol or drugs are more prone to becoming physically and emotionally abusive than parents who are not, and (2) being alcohol- or drug-dependent often causes a parent to be unavailable to care for or supervise their children
  • Parents who lack empathy for victims
  • Parents who have a history of having been abused themselves

The information in this post is not intended to be a criticism of parents. If you recognize your family environment or recognize your own behavior, take this post as a warning for how you can prevent sibling abuse from occurring in your family. Most importantly, if one or more of your children come to you complaining about a sibling emotionally, physically, or sexually abusing them—take them seriously and do something about it.

item.title: The Joy and Meaning of Living With City-Savvy Wild Creatures
item.description:
Environment

The Joy and Meaning of Living With City-Savvy Wild Creatures

Neha Sinha's new book finds wild neighbors in the most unexpected places.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • In her new book, Neha Sinha offers "brilliant and nuanced explorations of curiosity and belonging."
  • In today's world, it is easy and important to "get out into nature" even in busy, noisy, and polluted cities.
  • Paying attention to nature is an act of care and an act that can ground us and make us happier.
An Indian golden jackal in Delhi.
Source: Neha Sinha.

Many people live among amazing wildness in unexpected places, including noisy, bustling, dirty cities and in their own neighborhoods. Not everyone is privileged to live in wild environs and among the reasons I was attached to conservationist Neha Sinha's new highly-acclaimed book, My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital is that she shows how easy it is to get out into nature in unexpected places. In her beautifully written book, she "uncovers the wild creatures, ecological histories, and deep sense of meaning that can be found in any city—and indeed, any place—in the world.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write My Wild City?

Neha Sinha: I think My Wild City came to me through the braid of love and loss. There were many creatures I loved growing up – fireflies, hoopoes, Gyps vultures. They seemed so odd; I wondered how they would speak. The vulture would be polite and aloof; the firefly would be an absolute zinger, and the hoopoes looked like punks in suits. However, as I grew older, I realised these animals were gone from Delhi, and other places I looked at in India. I also realised we were suffering from generational amnesia – many of my peers did not even remember having seen them. Someone pointed at a (still abundant) Black kite and said: look, there’s your vulture. There are worldwide declines of migratory birds and fireflies, and Gypsy vultures are heavily impacted by the illegally used cattle-painkiller diclofenac.

What I loved seemed to be lost, but it was also a private loss, almost like grief, because others did not record it.

I realised then I needed to go on a quest to find these creatures again.

The book brings together love, loss and this quest, and also tries to create a new vocabulary for life through the lessons Nature offers us.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

NS: I hope to reach everyone who has never looked a wild animal in the eye, or has turned away, because they think animals and nature are something ‘far away’. In many ways, animals mess up the boundaries of our lives – in the way of mischievous cousins coming over for summer. There are jackals howling in the book, nilgai antelope running through campuses, civets and owls making the night their own, large native semal flowers plopping on cars in hospital parking lots, inconvenient but also providing levity – smudging all the order and borders we like to set up. The book suggests that opening our lives to these processes is opening our lives to new pathways of meaning, to a wilder, but ultimately more humourous and connected life.

Source: Chelsea Green/with permission.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

NS: I am concerned with ecological memories, and also the frail nature of memory – we remember some things, and forget others. It can be quite random. I remember a House sparrow nesting behind my grandfather’s oil painting every summer, until they just stopped, corresponding with House sparrow decline. Others don’t remember this. I feel, as do other nature writers, that we must mine our ecological memories, and record them, because if we don’t know what we have lost, we will never value it, and never try to restore it.

The second message of the book is that there is a lot of nature even in cities, despite our efforts to the contrary. Writers like JC Niala and Robert Macfarlane also write about how nature is where we are, and there is a wilderness within us that needs to be nurtured. Ultimately, the book talks about restoration of the native – of recreating habitat on the banks of the River Yamuna, of creating biodiversity parks. More parks, not parking lots; and more ecology and less of horticulture, in that we don’t want the same few garden plants being planted everywhere. We have over 400 bird species in Delhi, and I want this to be a source of pride, not another random fact.

The third message of the book is to find community to go outdoors. This book wouldn’t have been possible without the birders, rewilders, and explorers in my life. They are my family that I can lean on – in the blistering heat and the rain, through Covid and illness.

Finally, this is also a book about post Covid recovery. I draw an analogy about how native plants are thorny, spindly, but resilient. They have a kind of fierce beauty, and strong spines. That is how people can be too – we are climate survivors, Covid survivors, city survivors – and going outdoors and observing nature creates a much-needed resilience to life. Birdwatching can be a way of finding ‘restorative attention’ as Stephen and Rachel Kaplan put it. I am saying paying attention to nature is an act of care, an act that can ground us, make us stronger, happier.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

NS: My Wild City is ten years of my personal research and observations. And the book also deals with many of my own experiences navigating a city as a young woman. Cities are exhausting and exhilarating both, and being a woman going out in the dark has many challenges, safety being one of them. I have mostly read nature through male perspectives, and this offers a female one, and one which tries to explore what happens if you go beyond convention. So really the book is for anyone who might have felt bullied, or overlooked, or like a misfit. I find you can craft a life of personal meaning despite challenges. You can find belonging even in the bustle.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about their neighborhoods they will come to treat and animals and flora with more respect, dignity, and compassion?

NS: Yes! I want people to name the wildflowers around them, grow them in their gardens, and create ecological corridors through hundreds of gardens. I also want people to discover the industriousness of a bird like a pitta that makes a nest and raises her chicks at great cost, and with great intricate care. Dignity is a wonderful word you have used – yes, I want to award dignity to the non-human, to look at a plant beyond it being a weed, at an animal beyond it being a ‘nuisance’. To look at them as part of the rich tapestry of our lives, not someone else’s.

item.title: Can Suicide Have a Biological Basis?
item.description:
Suicide

Can Suicide Have a Biological Basis?

Could the biology of fear give us an insight into some deaths by suicide?

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Our society looks for someone to blame, but therapists cannot know whether someone will take their own life.
  • A long established theory linking suicide to recovering energy on emerging from depression remains unproven.
  • However, the workings of the fear system may offer a new perspective on this old theory.
Source: GDJ / Pixabay

As we get closer to World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10th, I want to share an idea on this subject. Few things, in my experience, create more stress for the therapist than working with a client who may be considering the possibility of suicide. It is unlikely, however, that any therapist will avoid this experience, and for some it may be a regular part of their work.

The context of blame and stress

We live in the context of a society that is prone to look for someone to blame when things go wrong. Health service managers and many agencies providing psychological therapies are often terrified of suicide, and, as a result, therapists are often not adequately supported in the aftermath. This comes on top of the natural anguish and self-questioning (Could I have done more?) that the therapist shares with family, loved ones and friends of the deceased, which is compounded by being subjected to stressful, blame-implying and time-consuming enquiries.

However much our society may wish to hold clinicians accountable for suicide prevention, we can’t avoid the fact that we simply don’t know if, or when, someone is going to die by suicide. Those who are most determined to take their own lives often stay quiet about it to ensure that no one can interfere. Do we have anything to go on to help us to reduce the risk of suicide in our clients beyond a history of previous attempts or the making of plans?

The energy-recovery theory

It has been accepted wisdom for many years that there is a particular risk of suicide in the early stages of recovery from depression. This view is often linked to the theory that as we recover from depression, we regain the energy that then makes a suicide attempt possible. A review of available data by Mittal and others[1] could not find evidence to support this view and concluded that this was a “plausible clinical hunch that remains unproven.” However, as the data examined appeared to offer no clear definition of what constituted recovery, it would seem that this accepted wisdom has not yet been clearly disproven.

I do think we should not be too hasty in dismissing the observations of generations of previous clinicians, and I wonder whether what we know of the functioning of the fear system may offer another perspective on their reflections.

A fear-system perspective

I have long wondered whether some suicide attempts might reflect a sudden emergence from the chronic energy shutdown of fear-collapse (the biological mechanism behind depression) into a powerful fear-arousal response, manifesting as a "disorganised fight-flight" reaction. This is what we see when a prey animal, which has been captured by a predator and has gone into shutdown, senses a window of opportunity to escape—Peter Levine gives a striking example of a mouse emerging from collapse actually attacking the cat that had caught it. This reaction was brought back to mind when one of my clients told me about her troubling fear-arousal response:

article continues after advertisement

Imogen, a woman in her early 60s, had been terrified by her cancer diagnosis and had undergone major surgery followed by chemotherapy. The chemotherapy had wiped her out for quite some time, but after the treatment finished, and she started to feel better, there was an incident that profoundly shook her. She completely lost her temper with her husband, shrieking at him and attacking him physically. She had never behaved in this way before and was shocked and distraught in the aftermath of the attack, thinking that she must be essentially evil to have behaved in this way. Having come across a similar response a few months previously, I shared the idea that had come to me on that occasion, that this might have been a "disorganised fight-flight" response arising as she emerged from the chronic collapse caused by her terror, the surgery and the impact of chemotherapy. I suggested that this was probably a normal biological response, and that it had been shown that the greater the fear at the commencement of collapse, the more powerful and disorganised was the manner of emerging from the collapse.[2] This simple explanation of something that had made no sense was a great relief to Imogen and calmed her distress.

This example led me to wonder whether this same mechanism activating in people more prone to turn anger into self-attack rather than a direct attack on others may underlie some suicide attempts seemingly coming out of the blue. This perspective appears to be compatible with the reflections of Schweizer and others[3] who hypothesized that suicide attempts might be more related to mood swings than to a resurgence of energy.

Is there a clinical application?

I wonder whether this hypothesis could help in safety-planning discussions with clients at risk of suicide, though I am doubtful about the practicality of psychoeducation during depressive shutdown owing to the impairment of cognitive function in this state.

However, the idea that a suicide attempt may reflect a disorganised fight-flight response upon emerging from depression may reconnect therapists with the “plausible clinical hunch” of past generations and prompt particular vigilance when clients show signs of emerging from depression.

article continues after advertisement

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Coming Home From War: PTSD May Not Tell the Full Story
item.description:
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

Coming Home From War: PTSD May Not Tell the Full Story

PTSD may not fully explain the challenges some veterans face after returning home.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • PTSD may not fully explain the severe challenges that some veterans experience after retuning from war zones.
  • Returning home physically after a life-threatening situation does not always mean coming home cognitively.
  • Cognitive immobility can leave us psychologically anchored to a life that has ended.
  • Cognitive immobility may help us better understand and support struggling veterans.

… we keep focusing on trauma, PTSD. But for a lot of these people, maybe it’s not trauma. I mean, certainly, soldiers are traumatized and the ones who are have to be treated for that. But a lot of them – maybe what’s bothering them is actually a kind of alienation. (Junger, TED Talk, 2015)

The quote above is from Sebastian Junger, an American journalist and author who has reported from conflict zones in Afghanistan, Africa, and the Middle East. It comes from his 2015 TED Talk, which has attracted more than 1.4 million views.

Junger's talk is a personal narrative of what he experienced after returning from Afghanistan, which is commonly regarded as PTSD, although he disputes this term. A reader sent it to me, and I was glad she did. I watched the talk several times and although I do not agree with him on every point, I find most of it compelling.

Junger was right to point out that what veterans battle with when they return home from a war zone may extend beyond PTSD or trauma. For many veterans, the resources available to support their PTSD often appear insufficient. This is evident in the high rate of suicide among veterans in both the UK and the United States. According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ 2025 report, 6,398 veterans died by suicide in 2023, an average of more than 17 deaths every day.

Junger also might be right that sometimes it is not what ex-soldiers have seen in war zones that torments them most and leads to many of them killing themselves, but what they experience upon returning. This relates to what a report in The Guardian observed: Veterans are “damaged [more] not by a traumatic event, but by the shock of returning from war.” It also connects to the idea that some people can come home only to discover that the home they left behind no longer exists in the same way; the emotional and social world that once made it feel like home is no longer available to them.

Junger’s suggestion was that the ‘alienation’ veterans suffer at home could be the result of their separation from the ‘tribe’ of their fellow soldiers. In my view, they are ‘alienated’ not just because they experience severe loneliness but because they cognitively remain in the war zone even though physically they have returned home.

This is what I call cognitive immobility—a state in which a person remains emotionally tied to a past life or experience even though their circumstances have changed. In this state they realise, sadly, that ‘… no home is truly a home; even the previous home – the ancestral home – has lost its distinguishing features and allure’ (Olumba, 2023, p.782).

PTSD vs. ‘Post-deployment alienation disorder’

Another comment of Junger's which captured my attention is that PTSD perhaps is the wrong term for what ex-soldiers who return from war experience.

I mean, maybe we just have the wrong word for some of it, and just changing our language, our understanding, would help a little bit: “Post-deployment alienation disorder”. Maybe even just calling it that for some of these people would allow them to stop imagining trying to imagine a trauma that didn’t really happen in order to explain a feeling that really is happening. And in fact, it’s an extremely dangerous feeling. That alienation and depression can lead to suicide. These people are in danger. It’s very important to understand why. (Junger, TED Talk, 2015)

Junger’s proposal was to replace the term PTSD with one like ‘Post-deployment alienation disorder’, to capture not just the trauma but also the ‘alienation’ he alluded to, while PTSD is a mental health condition which describes what persons who have experienced or witnessed a terrifying or life-threatening event go through.

article continues after advertisement

In my view, Junger’s term is too narrow to capture what goes on with anyone who has witnessed or lived through an experience that needs to be recorded deep in their memory. Emotionally charged experiences stay with us because we draw on that experience to survive similar situations in the future (Charan Ranganath, 2024).

The PTSD diagnosis has its purpose, but what the militaries of the USA, UK and other countries need to consider is differentiating between ex-soldiers ‘… who are haunted by memories of war but live in the present cognitively and those whose minds have never really left the battlefield, even after they receive effective treatment for PTSD’.

Those who live cognitively in the present may not long for their former military life, while others may wish to return to the war zone. This difference could lie in what persists and how it persists. With PTSD, people may live in the present while repeatedly re-experiencing traumatic events. With cognitive immobility, however, their cognitive and emotional orientation may remain anchored to their former military life.

Having that understanding may help us recognise the challenges that ex-soldiers face that do not fit neatly within familiar labels such as PTSD. Therefore, veterans who have received treatment for PTSD but still feel ‘alienated’ or unable to cognitively leave the war zone would then be given support that would help them live in the present. This is what we should be researching now in order to give them that support.

Final Thoughts

I agree with Junger that veterans living with what he describes as ‘post-deployment alienation disorder’ may be vulnerable to suicide, but I believe cognitive immobility may also help us understand what some of them are experiencing.

However, this experience is not confined to those returning from war. People going through heartbreak, divorce, imprisonment, bereavement, or displacement from their homeland or family may experience something similar. These are huge disruptions in life that someone may not have full control over.

article continues after advertisement

Healing may begin when we recognise that present distress is not always just about what happened to us but also about the difficulty of cognitively moving from what was to what is.

If we are to support people through such transitions, we may need, as Junger urged, to look beyond PTSD and consider not only why the mind can remain stuck in the past, but also what might help release it from the past into the present.

item.title: How to Find a Meaningful, Purposeful Focus
item.description:
Career

How to Find a Meaningful, Purposeful Focus

"Follow the buzz" to identify what deserves your attention.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Tuning into oneself requires open time and space.
  • Choosing a path that is right for you provides emotional sustenance.
  • Developing your own interests can be an antidote to social comparison.
Source: SIphotography/istockphoto

At work, my mentor said it’s a good idea to develop an area of interest. How do I know what’s right for me?

I don’t love my job, but I need the steady paycheck. I need to do something outside of work that feels meaningful to me. Or maybe I should just join a gym? I don’t even know …

All education and careers come with some amount of burdensome work. That is unavoidable. Sometimes the best option isn’t the most interesting, but the one that is most stable, or the one that provides a positive environment.

Then, there are moments in life when an area of concentration becomes possible, whether at work or during your free time. It can feel overwhelming when life provides possibilities, and you are supposed to sort through which one to choose. Deciding which path to travel is not inconsequential. Identifying an interest that will be sustaining can feel tricky.

In these situations, it’s easy to push up against “should”. I “should” specialize in this field because it will look good on my resume. I “should” be part of this project team because it is the most prestigious. I “should” spend my precious free time in a recommended activity, even though I don’t like it that much. The “should” focuses on outside forces, instead of looking inward.

To help identify a direction with meaning and purpose, I have a construct that I have used successfully throughout my career; I call it “Finding the Buzz”.

Identifying an Area of Enduring Interest

“Finding the buzz” means leaning into subjects or projects that you think about during spare open moments during the day. With our smartphones, it can be more difficult to tune into this experience, because “finding the buzz” requires quiet space so our mind has the opportunity to wander. If these moments are filled with ongoing engagement, whether social media scrolling or short videos, it can be harder to tune into oneself.

Once in the shower, walking to your car, or on your commute without constant distractions, what are you thinking about? In the quiet, where does your mind go? Is there something at work or a project at home that you might want to investigate?

Follow the musings that have a sense of play over those with anxious or ruminative circles. Pay attention to the question “I wonder what would happen if…”, especially if it leads to a sense of exploration, not worry. Once the spark is lit, one idea may lead to another, boosting enthusiasm and curiosity. Ask yourself: does it feel challenging and creative to think about this topic, or alternatively, does it feel depleting and burdensome?

Pursuing the Buzz Is Rejuvenating

As a therapist, I focus on building strengths and passions, in addition to understanding vulnerabilities and distress. In the office (identifying details changed), I cheer on a middle-aged woman who extracted herself from an abusive marriage and is now passionate about weight-lifting and the community it has provided. A 24-year-old struggles to find meaning after college, until she finds inspiration and joy pursuing modern dance and painting in her spare time. An electrician with an enduring side interest in politics was secure but bored in his job. He volunteered at a union meeting and ran into his buzz. He is considering a career shift to become a full-time union employee.

I have used this concept to guide my career with positive results. While much of medical training is pre-determined, there are moments when one can choose a side project. During specialty training, I was offered opportunities to do research, write a paper, or work on a book chapter. I couldn’t muster enthusiasm for any of these, although all would help forward my career.

Then, as I struggled to learn psychotherapeutic techniques, I commented to a wise supervisor that I would like to write a book on psychotherapy for beginners once I had more experience. “Let’s write it now together,” he proposed.

I started thinking about this idea while on the elevator on the wards, and in my evening spare time. I grabbed a composition book (which nowadays would be a Notes app) and filled it with questions and ideas. The buzz planted the seed for Becoming a Therapist: What Do I Say and Why, which I wrote with my mentor, Dr. Ed Messner. The project took six years to complete, but the work was inherently interesting to me, so I stayed engaged even when the grunt work was substantial.

Years later, I know a project (or a blog topic) is right for me if the concept acts as a catalyst and I start thinking about new angles or approaches to the idea during my free moments. This is my green light to move forward.

The pursuit of any endeavor has three sections. There is the first portion of the project when the excitement predominates; this is the creative surge with pop-up thoughts. Then, whatever the undertaking, the middle section is the most challenging. If it is writing and teaching, it is the strenuous work organizing ideas and editing. If it gardening, it is weeding. If it is learning a new skill, it is acquiring expertise, which requires sweat equity and lots of repetition. To maintain focus for the middle difficult section, it helps a great deal to have a buzz at the beginning. The feeling of opportunity, curiosity and interest fuels the pursuit. Then, at the end, it all comes together with a new ability or a final product.

A side benefit: identifying what is meaningful to you is protective in a world where we all have too much information about what others are doing or have done. Comparison and FOMO lose power if you are excited about your own choices. The prestige is internal. Confidence emerges when you are making the choices that are inherently valuable and interesting to you.

item.title: Artistic Twinships: Where Does Talent Come From?
item.description:
Understanding Twins

Artistic Twinships: Where Does Talent Come From?

Twins reveal the roots of artistic talents and collaboration.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Artistic talent reflects genetic factors and experience.
  • A study found that identical twins show greater resemblance in aptitude than fraternal twins.
  • Artistic collaboration involves compatible personalities. Identical twins show us the way.

What separates artists from people who appear to lack artistic talent? What enables some artists to collaborate creatively and productively? Answers to these questions may come from twin studies suggesting that a blend of genetic effects and compatible personalities is essential. A study in the Netherlands looked at twins’ within-pair similarity for music, the arts, writing, language, chess, mathematics, sports, memory, and knowledge and found that identical twins show greater resemblance in aptitude than fraternal twins. This pattern of results demonstrates genetic effects. Of course, practice, training, and opportunity are important for the expression and development of talent.

Collaboration Dynamics Among Artistic Twins

I have interviewed a number of identical twins and a pair of fraternal twins who work exceptionally well together. (Few collaborating fraternal twins were found, suggesting that they do not work together as often as do identical twins.) A recurrent theme is that these twins are mostly interested in the joint product, showing little concern for who contributed more or who contributed less. Twins usually do not seem to mind if their name is listed second on a book or publication, something that nontwin collaborators often have to decide in advance. They also express particular enjoyment working with their twin, over and beyond what they experience when working with someone outside their twinship.

In an earlier post here, I discussed the twin artists Dabid and Oieter Oyens, Josef and Menasch Seidenbeutal, and Ivan and Malvin Albright. Recently, I have come across other twin artists, so I will focus my attention on several selected pairs. I believe that we should take their comments seriously, as they may help everyone collaborate more effectively with family, friends, and co-workers, and tell us where our interests and talents come from.

Spotlights on Artistic Twins

Two pairs of artistic twins are worth noting as they are attracting considerable attention from critics. Simon and Nikolai Haas, from Austin, Texas, are 41 years old. These fraternal male twins have been working together on artistic creations since they were 15 (New York Times, 2026). They had a major breakthrough when they were in their 20s and Italian designer Donatella Versace gave them a commission that greatly furthered their career. They have now opened an exhibition titled “Haas Brothers: Uncanny Valley” at New York’s Museum of Arts and Design. They want to draw viewers into a different world—in their own words, they wish to offer an “alternative experience.”

It turns out that they share their artistic talents with their family members. The twins’ father was a stone carver and painter, their mother is an opera singer and screenwriter, and their older brother was a childhood actor. Interestingly, the interests and talents of their parents and sibling differ—perhaps the twins wanted to create a niche for themselves to distinguish themselves from the others.

Unfortunately, the Haas twins did not discuss their working relationship or their feelings about twinship. Fortunately, the Balbusso twins did.

Identical twins Anna and Elena Balbusso, from Italy, describe their working relationship as “symbiotic”—in other words, they “melt into a single multi-creative entity.” The twins have displayed their art on a number of occasions, but they are having their first New York exhibition at the Society of Illustrators. The show is titled Balbusso Twins: Illustrating With Two Souls and is on display until September 12, 2026. A look at the society’s website reveals duplicated figures, most probably twins.

The process of the Balbusso twins entails talking to one another on a continuous basis. They like flexibility in their work, unlike most illustrators who are encouraged to keep to the same style to gain recognition. They like to work on socially sensitive and timely topics, including civil rights, abortion, and violence against women. The twins expressed the quality of their relationship as follows: “We see and feel ourselves as different people, but we have always felt like twins. Being twins is an ancestral bond of deep love, maybe even stronger than the bond between a mother and child. It is a condition where 'we' comes before 'I.'” They added that they decided to work together to avoid competition between them.

A version of this post will also appear in the journal Twin Research and Human Genetics. The lives of additional collaborating twins representing different artistic and academic fields are documented in my forthcoming book, Twinship (2027).

item.title: Cannabidiol for Anxiety: What Does the Evidence Show?
item.description:
CBD

Cannabidiol for Anxiety: What Does the Evidence Show?

Evidence suggests potential benefits, but clinical results remain inconsistent.

Posted September 1, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety can have a significant impact on daily life and overall well-being.
  • CBD may affect biological systems involved in anxiety, stress, and fear.
  • Current evidence suggests potential benefits, but important questions remain unanswered.
  • More research is needed before CBD can be considered an established treatment for anxiety.
Source: CRYSTALWEED cannabis / Unsplash

Anxiety disorders are among the most common psychiatric conditions and can significantly affect quality of life. Although anxiety is a normal response to stress, anxiety disorders involve excessive or persistent fear and worry that interfere with everyday life.

Symptoms vary depending on the type of anxiety disorder, but may include:

  • Excessive or persistent worry
  • Fear or apprehension
  • Increased heart rate
  • Rapid breathing
  • Sweating
  • Fatigue
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Sleep disturbances

Because conventional treatments do not work equally well for everyone, researchers have been investigating whether cannabidiol (CBD), a non-intoxicating compound found in cannabis, could have a role in treating anxiety.

How does cannabidiol affect anxiety?

CBD does not produce the "high" associated with tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), another major cannabis compound. Laboratory and human studies suggest that CBD can affect several systems involved in anxiety and stress, including serotonin signaling and the endocannabinoid system.

However, the exact mechanisms behind its potential anxiolytic effects are still being investigated. More importantly, evidence from laboratory studies cannot automatically be translated into an effective treatment for anxiety disorders in humans.

What do recent studies show?

Research published since 2020 has provided some encouraging results, but it has also made the limitations of the evidence clearer.

A 2024 systematic review of randomized controlled trials identified 11 eligible studies. The researchers found that the results were inconsistent, partly because the studies differed considerably in the anxiety disorders studied, CBD doses, treatment duration, and methods used to measure anxiety. The authors concluded that CBD may reduce anxiety, but better-designed clinical trials are still needed.

Another systematic review and meta-analysis, also published in 2024, analyzed eight studies involving 316 participants. It found a significant reduction in anxiety among people receiving CBD compared with control groups. However, the authors emphasized that the small number of participants and limitations of the available studies make the findings difficult to interpret with confidence.

One of the more notable recent studies was a 15-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 178 people with mild to moderate anxiety disorders. Participants receiving a specific nanodispersible CBD formulation showed greater improvements in anxiety scores than those receiving placebo. The study reported no serious adverse events.

This result is encouraging, but it should be interpreted cautiously. Several authors of the study were employees or executives of companies involved in developing the CBD formulation, which represents a potential source of bias.

Other recent trials have produced less encouraging results. For example, a randomized placebo-controlled study of people with high levels of worry found that a single dose of CBD did not reduce anxiety or worry. After two weeks of treatment, 300 mg of CBD reduced some measures of anxiety but did not reduce worry, one of the central cognitive symptoms of anxiety.

Similarly, a 2024 randomized trial involving people exposed to trauma found that 300 mg of CBD did not significantly reduce anxiety, distress, or heart rate in response to trauma-related reminders.

Taken together, these findings suggest that CBD may have anxiolytic effects in some circumstances, but the evidence does not yet establish it as a reliable treatment for anxiety disorders.

Is CBD safe?

CBD is often described as harmless because it does not produce the intoxication associated with THC, but that does not mean it is free of risks. CBD can cause adverse effects and may interact with other medications. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also warned about the potential for liver injury and drug interactions. These concerns are particularly important for people taking medications regularly.

The quality and composition of commercially available CBD products can also vary. For example, a product labeled as CBD may contain different amounts of CBD than stated on the label and may contain other cannabinoids, including THC.

For these reasons, people taking medication should discuss CBD use with a healthcare professional rather than assuming that it is automatically safe because it is derived from a plant.

So, can CBD treat anxiety?

The answer is not yet clear.

Research has moved beyond the small case series and early studies available in 2020, and some newer clinical trials and meta-analyses suggest that CBD may reduce anxiety. At the same time, other well-controlled studies have found little or no benefit.

The most accurate conclusion at this point is that CBD is a promising but unproven treatment for anxiety disorders. Larger, independent clinical trials are still needed to determine which patients might benefit, what doses are appropriate, how long treatment should continue, and how CBD compares with established treatments.

CBD should therefore not be considered a replacement for evidence-based treatments for anxiety until stronger evidence is available.
